title: Northwind x Redwood - POC check-in (perf results + tail latency)
text:
summary:
POC weekly check-in focused on reviewing the benchmark spreadsheet (A100/H100/L40S runs) and explaining the p99 behavior for long-context summarization workloads. Redwood walked through how runtime 1.21 kernel auto-selection v2 behaves across seq-length buckets and why one L40S result set showed a tail spike likely due to a mis-bucket / fallback kernel on long prefill. Customer asked about determinism, how to reproduce selection decisions, and what knobs exist to pin/override kernels during rollout. Team aligned on running a dedicated pool test on an H100-only pool first (then mixed A100), using Northwind’s actual prompt distribution and a fixed concurrency target, with Redwood providing the exact runtime flags/telemetry queries and an allowlist config to keep v2 controlled.

topics:
Benchmark spreadsheet review: p50/p95/p99 latency deltas vs baseline
Long-context prefill vs decode behavior and seq-length bucketing
GPU SKU differences (H100 vs A100 80GB vs L40S) and stability
Kernel auto-selection v2 determinism, telemetry, and sampling overhead
Plan for a Dedicated pool test and rollout guardrails / rollback

questions:
For long-context (16k–32k) prompts, what specific kernel is being selected and can we force it for an A/B run?
If we move to Dedicated, can we request an H100-only pool and avoid mixed SKUs during the POC?
How do we know selection decisions are deterministic across restarts / across hosts?
What are the rollback triggers you recommend (p99 delta threshold, error rate)?
Can Redwood share the exact dashboard queries / fields to break down p99 by seq bucket and GPU SKU?

next_steps:
Redwood to send a sanitized export of the benchmark table with notes on the L40S anomaly and the long-context bucket definitions.
Northwind to provide a 24h histogram of prompt lengths (prefill tokens) and target concurrency / throughput goal for the dedicated test.
Redwood to set up a Dedicated trial plan for an H100-only pool and propose a 2-hour canary window to run the same scenario suite.
Redwood to share runtime flags for selection tracing + a minimal telemetry sampling config suitable for POC.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up after the dedicated run to review p99 and decide on next model/GPU configuration.

action_items:
Markus Klein (Redwood) - Email dedicated pool options + proposed H100 SKU(s) and region choices - Due 2026-02-20
Isabella Rossi (Redwood) - Add annotation in the spreadsheet for the L40S long-prefill run (suspected fallback kernel) + rerun microbench if needed - Due 2026-02-21
Omar El-Sayed (Redwood) - Send telemetry field list + dashboard links/queries for kernel selection breakdown (model/GPU/seq bucket) - Due 2026-02-20
Priya Shah (Northwind) - Share prompt-length distribution + current p99 SLO target and acceptable regression budget - Due 2026-02-20
Nina Patel (Northwind) - Confirm whether any driver/CUDA constraints exist in their environment for Private later (even if Dedicated first) - Due 2026-02-24

transcript:
Meeting: Northwind x Redwood - POC check-in (perf results + tail latency)
Recorded: 2026-02-19 16:00 PST
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees:
- Markus Klein (Redwood)
- Omar El-Sayed (Redwood)
- Isabella Rossi (Redwood)
- Lauren Bishop (Redwood)
- Priya Shah (Northwind)
- David Lin (Northwind)
- Nina Patel (Northwind)
- Tom Becker (Northwind)

Auto-generated notes (may be inaccurate)
Summary: Reviewed benchmark spreadsheet and tail latency concerns. Aligned on dedicated pool test plan (H100 first) with controlled rollout of kernel selection v2.

Transcript

[00:00] Markus (Redwood): Hey everyone. Can you all hear me okay?
[00:03] Priya (Northwind): Yep, good.
[00:04] Omar (Redwood): Yeah, loud and clear.
[00:06] Tom (Northwind): Yep.
[00:07] Markus (Redwood): Cool. So today we said we’d spend most of the time on the perf sheet you all were updating and specifically the p99 questions on long-context summarization. Isabella’s here because she was looking at the SKU-specific stuff, and Omar can talk telemetry and the tail.
[00:22] Priya (Northwind): Great. We have the spreadsheet open. The tab “v1 vs v2 - Feb 18” is the one.

[00:30] Isabella (Redwood): Yep, I’m on that tab. I might reference row numbers but… I know they move.
[00:35] David (Northwind): No worries.

[00:38] Markus (Redwood): Priya, do you want to recap what you’re seeing that’s worrying you?
[00:43] Priya (Northwind): Sure. So overall the median is fine, p50 is like better in most cases. But the p99 on the 16k to 32k bucket, on L40S specifically, jumped. It’s like, I wrote down, baseline p99 was ~2.1 seconds and then v2 run is like 2.9, 3.0 seconds. It’s enough that it would blow our internal SLO if that’s real.
[01:05] Nina (Northwind): And just to add, it’s not every run. It was like one of the canary runs. But it’s scary because in production you don’t get to pick when you hit the p99.

[01:16] Omar (Redwood): Yep. That’s the right instinct. Tail is where surprises hide.
[01:19] Isabella (Redwood): Also just to sanity check, that’s the “long prefill, short decode” scenario right? The summarization prompts that are huge inputs but then you only generate like, what, 200 tokens.
[01:28] David (Northwind): Exactly. We pass a big document, ask for structured summary, output is short.

[01:34] Omar (Redwood): Okay. So the important nuance: that workload is dominated by prefill, not decode. A lot of people mentally map “LLM latency” to decode tokens/sec, but here it’s prefill time. Kernel selection v2 explicitly buckets based on a prefill/decode regime signal. If that signal mis-classifies a request—like it thinks it’s a balanced decode workload—it can pick a kernel that’s great for steady decode but not great for huge prefill.
[01:58] Priya (Northwind): That’s basically what we’re worried about. So is this misclassification, or is it just L40S being like… weaker?

[02:06] Isabella (Redwood): I think it’s a combo. L40S is a different memory and different “best” kernel in the long prefill. But in the run you’re pointing at, the candidate set for L40S had one kernel denylists in our internal notes for a specific driver. I’m not 100% sure what driver you were on.
[02:22] Nina (Northwind): We used the default in your image. I think it was CUDA 12.2? Driver… I can pull it.
[02:28] Markus (Redwood): That’d help. We also can send you the “print runtime env” command so it’s in the logs.

[02:35] Priya (Northwind): But even if it’s driver, our reality is we might land on those drivers in Dedicated too, unless we control it.
[02:42] Lauren (Redwood): In Dedicated we can control the driver stack per pool, yes. That’s one of the benefits. We can say “H100 pool with driver X” and keep it pinned during POC.
[02:52] Tom (Northwind): That’s helpful.

[02:55] Omar (Redwood): Let me propose how to interpret the sheet. If you look at H100 numbers: p95 and p99 improved or stayed flat across most buckets. A100 also mostly improved. The L40S has the outlier in long prefill. That pattern suggests it’s not “v2 is generally unstable”, it’s “on that SKU and regime, one selection path is suboptimal”. Which is fixable with allow/deny rules, and also by making the long-prefill threshold more conservative.

[03:20] Priya (Northwind): So for our POC, can we just… avoid L40S? Because we don’t need it. We’d rather spend money on fewer, faster GPUs and have stable tail.
[03:28] Markus (Redwood): Yes, that’s exactly what we were going to suggest. Start with H100-only dedicated pool, run your scenario suite, validate p99. Then optionally test A100 80GB if cost matters. L40S is more “cost optimized” but it’s not necessary for your first pass.
[03:44] David (Northwind): We put L40S in because we saw it in some public benchmarks and it’s available in our cloud account, but we can drop it.

[03:53] Isabella (Redwood): And to be clear, we don’t have a philosophical issue with L40S, it’s just more sensitive to kernel choice in the long-prefill case.

[04:01] Nina (Northwind): Okay, but long term, if we did end up with mixed fleets, how does v2 handle heterogenous? Like will it pick different kernels for different SKUs consistently?
[04:10] Omar (Redwood): Yes. v2 keys on GPU SKU, model family, and seq bucket. That’s the “three-axis” thing. So the decision is not “one kernel for all”. It’s “for this model family, on this GPU type, in this regime, pick kernel K”. And we emit telemetry so you can actually see the distribution.

[04:29] Priya (Northwind): We saw in the notes from last time something about determinism. Can you clarify that? We had a bad experience elsewhere where the “auto tuning” changed its mind.
[04:38] Omar (Redwood): Totally. We’re not doing online learned tuning in the hot path. It’s rule-based plus a registry. So given the same inputs—model hash/version, GPU SKU normalized, and the extracted seq regime—you get the same decision. There’s no randomness. The only way it changes is if you change the config or the registry version, or you roll out a new runtime.
[04:59] David (Northwind): What about, like, if the scheduler passes in “observed distribution hints” and that changes over time? Does that change selection?
[05:07] Omar (Redwood): Good catch. There is an optional hint channel. In Dedicated we can either turn it off or keep it read-only for stability. And even if it’s on, it’s still deterministic per window, but the window could drift if your traffic mix changes. For your POC we can lock it down: use request-local features only, no adaptive hints.
[05:27] Priya (Northwind): That sounds good. Lock it down please.

[05:30] Markus (Redwood): Isabella, can you walk through what you think happened in that L40S spike? Like, plain English.
[05:36] Isabella (Redwood): Yeah. So the long-context run: you have big input, short output. v2 tries to detect that and chooses a “prefill-optimized” kernel. On H100/A100 it does. On L40S, the registry has a fallback order. One of the candidates is “fast in median” but has a tail risk when prefill is huge and the workspace gets tight. If it falls back to that kernel—either because the preferred kernel is missing for that driver or it’s marked unstable—then you see occasional long outliers.
[06:06] Nina (Northwind): Workspace gets tight meaning memory?
[06:09] Isabella (Redwood): Yeah, like scratch memory and sometimes you get fragmentation. I’m simplifying, but yes.

[06:15] Priya (Northwind): So if we do H100-only, we basically bypass this whole path.
[06:20] Isabella (Redwood): Pretty much.

[06:23] Tom (Northwind): Okay. But how do we trust that H100 won’t have some other weird corner? We don’t have a huge test budget.
[06:32] Omar (Redwood): We can define clear canary criteria. For example: run 30 minutes of your workload replay on the dedicated pool with v2 on, compare against v1 pinned kernel selection or v1 selector. We set thresholds: p99 must be within, say, +3% of baseline or better; error rate must not increase; and the selection distribution should be stable. If any threshold trips, we flip the gate.
[06:57] Priya (Northwind): When you say “flip the gate”, you mean we can disable v2 without redeploying?
[07:02] Lauren (Redwood): Yes. In Dedicated, it’s a config toggle per model / per pool. It’s basically hot reload.
[07:08] Nina (Northwind): That’s good.

[07:10] David (Northwind): Can we also force a kernel just for the experiment? Like A/B exact same kernel and see if it’s selection overhead.
[07:18] Isabella (Redwood): Yes. There’s a CLI flag that forces kernel choice and can dump the selection trace. I’ll send you the exact flag name after this. It’s something like `--force_kernel=` and `--dump_selector_trace`.
[07:31] Omar (Redwood): And selection overhead is tiny, like microseconds to low milliseconds depending on sampling. The bigger overhead is telemetry if you log every request. So we sample. For POC we can do 0.1% sampling but always sample “slow requests” above a threshold.
[07:49] Priya (Northwind): Always sample slow ones would be ideal.

[07:52] Markus (Redwood): Let’s talk dedicated plan. Lauren, can you outline what we can offer in terms of GPUs and regions for the next week?
[08:00] Lauren (Redwood): Yeah. In us-west we can do an 8xH100 pool pretty quickly, or a 4xH100 if you want smaller. Alternatively A100 80GB is more plentiful. My recommendation: 4xH100 first for the test, because your traffic in POC is not huge. Then if you want to scale and see throughput stability, we can expand to 8x.
[08:22] Tom (Northwind): We’d rather do 4 first.
[08:25] Priya (Northwind): Agreed.

[08:27] Nina (Northwind): Any chance of H100 PCIe vs SXM differences? We’ve seen those show up.
[08:33] Isabella (Redwood): Good question. Yes, there are differences. In our registry we normalize SKU. But the dedicated offering is typically H100 SXM for the 8x nodes. For 4x, it can vary. Lauren, what’s available?
[08:47] Lauren (Redwood): For the trial we can do SXM in an 8x chassis but allocate you 4 GPUs worth of capacity, or we do a smaller PCIe node. It depends on the timing. I’ll confirm and email.
[09:00] Priya (Northwind): Please confirm. We’d prefer consistency over absolute cheapest.

[09:07] Markus (Redwood): Okay. Now, spreadsheet. David, you ran the mixed workload too, right? The one with 70% short prompts, 30% long docs.
[09:16] David (Northwind): Yeah. That one looked fine. p99 didn’t move much. That’s why we were confused why the long-only scenario spiked.
[09:25] Omar (Redwood): That actually fits. In mixed workloads, the scheduler batching can smooth some of the tail. But in long-only, every request is heavy prefill and you can’t “hide” the worst case behind cheap ones.
[09:39] Nina (Northwind): Also in mixed you might have fewer concurrent long ones, depending on arrival.
[09:44] Omar (Redwood): Exactly.

[09:46] Priya (Northwind): For our production, it’s mostly long-only during certain hours. It’s batch summarization.
[09:52] Markus (Redwood): That’s important. So our POC should mirror that: sustained long-only, steady concurrency.

[10:00] Tom (Northwind): What concurrency are you thinking?
[10:03] Priya (Northwind): Our job runner typically does 32 concurrent docs per worker cluster. But we can scale.
[10:10] Omar (Redwood): Let’s pick a target throughput. For example “X docs/minute at p99 < Y seconds”. If you tell us your SLO and volume, we can propose concurrency.
[10:22] Priya (Northwind): Our internal SLO is p99 under 2.4 seconds for the 16k-32k bucket. Volume is like 200k docs/day but it’s spiky.
[10:34] Markus (Redwood): Got it.

[10:36] David (Northwind): Also, we’re doing structured output. Does that change kernel selection? It shouldn’t, but just asking.
[10:43] Isabella (Redwood): It shouldn’t affect kernel selection, no. That’s more on decoding constraints and logit processing, but kernel selection is at attention / matmul level and depends on shapes.

[10:56] Priya (Northwind): So what do we need to provide you before you can set up the dedicated test?
[11:01] Lauren (Redwood): Two things: region preference, and whether you need any special networking like VPC peering for the POC. If it’s just hitting the dedicated endpoint over TLS, we can start without private networking.
[11:13] Nina (Northwind): For the POC, public endpoint is fine. For prod we’ll want VPC, but not for this.
[11:19] Lauren (Redwood): Great, that speeds it up.

[11:22] Omar (Redwood): And from the perf side, we need the prompt length distribution and the exact “max output tokens” you set. Because that affects the prefill/decode regime signal.
[11:33] David (Northwind): We can share a histogram. We have it in Datadog. I can export.
[11:38] Priya (Northwind): I’ll send it.

[11:41] Markus (Redwood): Let’s do the tail latency mechanics question: How do we verify the kernel selection per request? Omar?
[11:48] Omar (Redwood): There are two methods. One is telemetry: we emit a “kernel_selection” event with fields like selected kernel id, gpu sku, model family tag, seq bucket, and whether it was fallback. That can be sampled. Two is local reproduction: enable trace dump on a specific request id. In Dedicated we can set “always dump on slow request” threshold, like >p95.
[12:15] Nina (Northwind): Is that trace dump PII-safe?
[12:18] Omar (Redwood): We don’t dump token content by default. It’s shapes and ids. But we can confirm the fields. You can also keep it internal to your account.

[12:29] Priya (Northwind): In the spreadsheet, can we add a column “chosen kernel” for each run?
[12:33] Isabella (Redwood): Yes, that’s actually a great idea. For the rerun, we can export the distribution: like 80% kernel A, 20% fallback kernel B. That might explain p99.

[12:46] Markus (Redwood): Okay. Quick competitor question that came up internally: you mentioned you tried Bedrock and Together. Anything relevant you want to share? It helps us tailor.
[12:56] Priya (Northwind): Bedrock was easy but we couldn’t get consistent tail on long inputs, and also the model choice was limited. Together was faster on average but we had occasional “mystery slow” and it was hard to debug. That’s why we like the idea of you showing us the kernel selection and stuff.
[13:14] Omar (Redwood): Makes sense.

[13:16] Tom (Northwind): Our leadership is basically asking “can we predict cost and SLO reliably”. Tail is the trust thing.
[13:23] Markus (Redwood): Understood.

[13:25] Nina (Northwind): So dedicated test. Will we be on runtime 1.21?
[13:29] Lauren (Redwood): Yes. Dedicated trial would be on 1.21 with v2 available, but we can start with v1 default and then do a controlled switch.
[13:39] Priya (Northwind): We’d like to start with v1 pinned, then turn v2 on as A/B.
[13:44] Isabella (Redwood): Perfect. We can do that.

[13:48] Omar (Redwood): And we can keep an allowlist: only your model gets v2, and only on H100, and only for your account.
[13:56] David (Northwind): Nice.

[14:00] Markus (Redwood): Let’s revisit the actual numbers. Isabella, can you call out the H100 p99 delta in long prefill scenario?
[14:07] Isabella (Redwood): In your sheet, H100 long prefill: p99 went from ~1.65s to ~1.52s, so about 8% improvement. Throughput was also a bit more stable. A100 was more modest, like 3-5%. L40S had the regression you mentioned.
[14:27] Priya (Northwind): That’s encouraging.

[14:29] Nina (Northwind): And any correctness differences? Like output changes?
[14:34] Markus (Redwood): Kernel selection should not change outputs. It’s deterministic math, same precision mode. We also run conformance tests. But we can include a quick output diff check in the POC harness.
[14:47] David (Northwind): We did spot check. Seems identical.

[14:52] Omar (Redwood): One caveat: if you’re using non-deterministic CUDA settings, you can see tiny floating point differences. But our runtime pins determinism settings in production mode.
[15:03] Priya (Northwind): Okay.

[15:05] Tom (Northwind): What’s your recommended rollback trigger during our POC? Just p99 or also error rate?
[15:12] Omar (Redwood): Both. Specifically: (1) p99 regression above 5% for 10 minutes in the long-context bucket, (2) error rate increase above baseline +0.2% absolute, (3) any spike in timeouts. And we also look at selection distribution: if fallback rate jumps, that’s an early warning.
[15:36] Nina (Northwind): Can we get those as alerts?
[15:39] Omar (Redwood): Yes, we can configure a dashboard and alerting. For POC we might do manual monitoring plus a simple alert.

[15:49] Priya (Northwind): Sampling: we don’t want to pay a ton of overhead. What sampling rate did you say?
[15:55] Omar (Redwood): 0.1% is typical. But for a POC, we can do 1% for a short run. The overhead is mostly log volume. The actual selector is not the cost.
[16:08] David (Northwind): If we do 1% for 2 hours that’s fine.

[16:12] Markus (Redwood): Sounds like we’re converging. Any other open concerns?
[16:17] Priya (Northwind): The only other thing: GPU naming. In the sheet we wrote “A100” but there are like, 40GB, 80GB, MIG, etc. We want to be sure we’re comparing apples to apples.
[16:30] Isabella (Redwood): Yeah. We’ve had confusion there too. In telemetry we normalize the SKU string and include memory size and whether MIG is enabled. For Dedicated we will avoid MIG for this test.
[16:43] Nina (Northwind): Please avoid MIG.
[16:45] Lauren (Redwood): Yep.

[16:47] Tom (Northwind): Timeline: can we do the dedicated test next week?
[16:52] Lauren (Redwood): I believe so. If we can get approval today, we can aim for Tuesday or Wednesday. Markus and I will follow up with exact times.
[17:02] Priya (Northwind): Tuesday works.

[17:05] Omar (Redwood): For the long-context anomaly, we’re also going to rerun that L40S scenario internally with a stricter long-prefill threshold, just to confirm it goes away. But again, you don’t need L40S for the decision.
[17:21] Priya (Northwind): Appreciate it.

[17:23] (crosstalk)
[17:24] Speaker 1: Sorry, one sec—
[17:25] Nina (Northwind): Go ahead, David.
[17:27] David (Northwind): Just wondering: do you cache the kernel selection per model and bucket? Like to avoid recomputing per request.
[17:35] Isabella (Redwood): Yes, there’s a cache keyed on (model, gpu sku, seq bucket, a couple flags). So after warmup it’s basically a lookup.
[17:45] David (Northwind): Great.

[17:47] Markus (Redwood): Okay, let’s outline the concrete plan.
[17:50] Markus (Redwood): Step 1: Northwind sends us prompt length histogram, max output tokens, and target p99 SLO. Step 2: Redwood provisions 4xH100 Dedicated in us-west, confirm SXM vs PCIe. Step 3: We run baseline with v1 pinned selection for 30 minutes. Step 4: Enable v2 gate for your model only, run same load. Step 5: Compare p95/p99 and selection distribution; decide go/no-go.

[18:18] Priya (Northwind): That’s good.
[18:20] Nina (Northwind): What tool do you want us to use to generate load? We have Locust.
[18:25] Omar (Redwood): Locust is fine. We can also provide a simple Python harness. But use what you already trust.
[18:33] Priya (Northwind): We’ll use our harness.

[18:36] Lauren (Redwood): On networking, since it’s public endpoint for now, you can start as soon as the pool is up.
[18:42] Tom (Northwind): Great.

[18:44] Omar (Redwood): I’ll send you the telemetry fields and a couple queries: break down p99 by seq bucket, and show fallback rate by GPU. Also a “top kernels by count” view.
[18:58] Priya (Northwind): Perfect.

[19:01] Markus (Redwood): Any procurement blockers for the dedicated trial?
[19:05] Tom (Northwind): Not yet. We’re still in evaluation. If this looks good, we’ll move fast.
[19:10] Markus (Redwood): Okay.

[19:12] Priya (Northwind): One last question: does enabling v2 change cost?
[19:16] Markus (Redwood): Not directly. It may reduce latency which often reduces GPU time per request, so cost could improve. But pricing is based on the dedicated commit, not per request.
[19:28] Priya (Northwind): Right.

[19:30] Nina (Northwind): For hosted vs dedicated: if we decide dedicated, we still can keep the same API surface?
[19:35] Lauren (Redwood): Yes, same API, different endpoint and capacity guarantees.

[19:41] (pause)
[19:42] Markus (Redwood): Cool. We’ve got about 5 minutes—anything else on the tail latency explanation that we didn’t cover?
[19:49] Priya (Northwind): No, that was clear. The main takeaway is: start H100-only, keep deterministic, use allowlist, and monitor fallback rate.
[19:58] Omar (Redwood): Exactly.

[20:01] Markus (Redwood): Great. We’ll follow up via email with (1) the dedicated pool details, (2) the updated spreadsheet notes, and (3) the telemetry/query bundle. Thanks everyone.
[20:12] Priya (Northwind): Thanks.
[20:13] Nina (Northwind): Thank you.
[20:14] Tom (Northwind): Thanks all.

(Transcript continued with light scheduling / goodbye chatter)

[20:20] Lauren (Redwood): Priya, Tuesday morning or afternoon works better?
[20:23] Priya (Northwind): Afternoon.
[20:25] Markus (Redwood): Okay we’ll propose 2pm PT.
[20:28] Priya (Northwind): Sounds good.
[20:30] Omar (Redwood): I’ll get you the queries today.
[20:32] Priya (Northwind): Great.

End of recording

title: Northwind Analytics (LLM)
text:
notes:
Account summary
- Northwind evaluating Redwood for long-context summarization of customer-owned datasets (reports, tickets, PDFs). Primary pain today is tail latency variability and cost predictability when requests swing between short prompts and very long-context summarization.
- They are currently prototyping on a mix of managed endpoints + internal GPU nodes; want a consistent runtime + clearer operational knobs.

Use case / workload
- Workload: long-context summarization ("quarterly narrative" + "case timeline") and some doc-search/embedding for retrieval.
- Context window requirements: routinely 16k–32k tokens; target to support 64k for a subset (exec summaries / consolidated case bundles).
- Traffic pattern: bursty during end-of-month reporting; mixed workloads (short interactive + long offline jobs) hitting same service unless we split pools.
- Latency: p50 is acceptable; main concern is p95/p99 spikes during long-context prefill ("prefill dominates; decode is secondary").
- Output constraints: deterministic-ish behavior preferred for compliance re-runs; wants ability to reproduce results in audits (same model + same runtime settings).

GPU / deployment constraints
- They cannot standardize on H100 in 2026H1. Current constraint: L40S for most capacity; some A100 in a separate region. (Asked multiple times if kernel behavior differs by SKU and how we prevent mis-selection.)
- Preference is VPC deployment for production (data residency + controlled egress). They will accept Hosted API for early dev, but want the same model+runtime config surface carried into Dedicated/VPC.
- Asked about MIG and SKU naming ambiguity in clouds; wants us to be explicit in how we detect/normalize GPU type and driver/CUDA combos.

Kernel selection v2 questions (key theme)
- They have heard about kernel auto-selection v2 in runtime 1.21 and asked how it decides between kernels for long-context vs mixed workloads.
- Specific questions from calls:
  - "How do you bucket sequence lengths—do you look at prompt vs decode separately?"
  - "If the selector gets it wrong, how fast can we pin a kernel or roll back? Is it per model? per GPU?"
  - "Is selection deterministic given the same inputs, or can two identical requests pick different kernels?"
  - "What telemetry do we get back to explain why a kernel was chosen?"
- We explained the plan: SKU-aware mapping + feature gates + allow/deny lists; selection telemetry (chosen kernel + candidate set + feature signals) sampled to avoid overhead; and explicit fallbacks when kernels are missing/unstable on a SKU.

Security / compliance notes
- Requirements flagged: SSO/SAML (Okta), audit logs exportable to their SIEM, KMS integration, configurable retention controls, and data residency (US-only for first phase).
- They will run a standard security review during POC if we move to a VPC/Dedicated test.

POC plan (proposed)
- Timeline (agreed direction, dates still being pinned):
  - Week of 2026-03-03: Dedicated pool smoke test (L40S-first) + baseline on v1 selector.
  - Week of 2026-03-10: Enable kernel selection v2 behind allowlist for the summarization model(s); compare p95/p99 + throughput stability on mixed workloads.
  - Week of 2026-03-17: Add A100 pool run + long-context (32k/64k) stress; validate no correctness regressions; document any pin/denylist rules needed.
  - End of March: security review + commercial proposal if perf is green.

Recent activity timeline
- 2026-02-05 (Fireflies): technical deep dive on runtime performance + kernel selection; discussed GPU SKU sensitivity, determinism expectations, and how overrides would work in a Dedicated/VPC setting.
- 2026-02-12 (Gmail thread): internal Redwood risk review re: runtime 1.21 + kernel auto-selection v2 rollout safety; shared high-level approach and emphasized feature gates + rapid rollback.
- 2026-02-19 (Fireflies): POC check-in; reviewed preliminary perf table (v1 vs v2) and highlighted one long-context anomaly; agreed to rerun with L40S-specific settings and stricter workload separation.
- 2026-02-24: Northwind sent initial GPU inventory + driver/CUDA versions; asked for a written runbook-style summary ("what to do if p99 spikes") for their oncall.

Risks / watchouts

title: Technical deep dive - runtime performance + kernel selection (Redwood x Northwind)

Fireflies.ai - Meeting Transcript

Title: Technical deep dive - runtime performance + kernel selection (Redwood x Northwind)
Date: 2026-02-05
Time: 10:00 AM - 10:56 AM PT
Duration: 56 minutes
Meeting ID: ff-20260205-ntw-td-9931

Attendees
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference)
- Omar El-Sayed (Redwood Inference)
- Yuki Sato (Redwood Inference)
- Ethan Park (Redwood Inference)
- Priya Nair (Northwind Analytics)
- Danielle Chen (Northwind Analytics)
- Alex Romero (Northwind Analytics)
- Tom Bowers (Northwind Analytics)

Summary (auto-generated)
Northwind asked for a deeper walkthrough of how Redwood selects GPU kernels at runtime, specifically around long-context summarization workloads and heterogeneous GPU fleets. Redwood explained kernel auto-selection v2 signals (model family/arch tags, sequence-length regime, GPU SKU normalization), fallback hierarchy, determinism guarantees, and rollout safety controls (feature gates, per-model allow/deny lists, rapid rollback, manual pinning). The group aligned on running a small benchmark matrix on A100 and L40S, with realistic prompt/decode distributions and tail latency monitoring.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Kernel selection: what it is, where it runs, and what inputs it uses
- GPU SKU mapping (A100 variants, MIG, cloud instance naming)
- Long-context performance: prefill vs decode regime and tail latency risk
- Safety mechanisms: fallbacks, determinism/replay, gates, rollback
- Benchmark plan + what data Northwind needs to provide

Questions (auto-generated)
- How do you prevent non-deterministic selection decisions across replicas?
- Can we force/pin a kernel for a specific model and GPU in Dedicated?
- What happens if a kernel is missing or unstable on one SKU?
- How do you detect long-context misclassification before it hits p99?

Transcript

[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, cool. Folks can hear me okay?

[00:03] Priya Nair: Yep, loud and clear.

[00:05] Markus Klein: Great. Thanks everyone for making time. This one is intended to be more technical than our last call. Omar and Yuki are here from runtime, Ethan from control plane. We can go deep on kernel selection, especially long context.

[00:18] Danielle Chen: Perfect. Yeah, we’re basically trying to de-risk tail latency. Our summarization jobs are like, 12k to 30k input tokens, and then maybe 300 to 1200 output tokens. It’s prefill heavy.

[00:30] Omar El-Sayed: Yep, that’s the classic “prefill dominates” shape. And that’s exactly where bad kernel choice shows up as p99 spikes, not necessarily average.

[00:39] Tom Bowers: And just to set context, we’re an enterprise. We have to answer questions like, can you roll back quickly and can we control it per region. We can’t just yolo a new thing.

[00:49] Markus Klein: Totally. That’s why we wanted Ethan on.

[00:52] Alex Romero: Also we’re comparing to… we’ve tested vLLM on our side, and TensorRT-LLM on a few nodes. So we’re trying to understand what Redwood’s doing differently, or what knobs we’ll get.

[01:03] Markus Klein: Makes sense. Omar, do you wanna start with the “what is kernel selection” for us, like the two-minute overview?

[01:10] Omar El-Sayed: Sure. So, in our runtime we have multiple kernel implementations for key parts of attention and related ops. Depending on model architecture and workload regime, different kernels win. Kernel auto-selection is the module that picks, for a given request, which kernel variant to run.

[01:27] Omar El-Sayed: In v2 specifically, we key selection on three buckets of signals: one, model family/architecture tags (like Llama-style vs Mistral-style, Qwen variants, Gemma-ish), two, sequence-length regime which we treat separately for prefill vs decode behavior, and three, GPU SKU, because H100 vs A100 vs L40S can change the winner.

[01:51] Priya Nair: When you say “request”, do you literally decide per request? Or per model load, like at startup?

[01:57] Yuki Sato: Good question. We decide at request time, but in practice we cache decisions. The selector outputs a decision based on a normalized feature vector. Most of those are stable for many requests: model id + gpu sku + seq bucket. So it’s more like “per regime,” not every time doing heavy computation.

[02:18] Danielle Chen: And your v1 did what?

[02:21] Yuki Sato: v1 was simpler, basically a mostly static mapping keyed on model class and a couple hard-coded thresholds. It didn’t account for SKU differences well, and it treated sequence length too coarsely. It worked for the middle of the distribution but we saw edge cases on long context.

[02:39] Omar El-Sayed: And also v1 had weaker observability. So when you got a latency spike, you couldn’t easily answer “which kernel did we pick” without attaching a profiler.

[02:49] Alex Romero: So v2 is rules? Or some ML thing?

[02:53] Yuki Sato: Rules. We debated a learned scorer, but for safety and explainability and rollback, we landed on rule-based with explicit fallbacks. It’s still a “scoring” concept internally, but it’s deterministic rules and precedence, not a trained model.

[03:10] Priya Nair: Deterministic… like, identical inputs always produce identical output kernel choice?

[03:15] Yuki Sato: Yes. Given the same model metadata, same GPU normalized SKU, same seq bucket inputs, you get the same selection. We’ve added replay tests to ensure that. We also version the rules so if we change thresholds, it’s tracked.

[03:30] Tom Bowers: What about multi-tenant? Like if another customer is running something weird, does it influence our selection?

[03:35] Omar El-Sayed: No. There’s no global learning. The only “dynamic” input can be scheduler hints about observed seq distribution, but those are local to the pool and still deterministic given the hint input. And you can disable that if you want.

[03:49] Ethan Park: Also from the control plane side, for Dedicated you can lock policy. You can say “always use v1 selector” or “use v2 only for these models.” There’s no cross-account mixing.

[04:01] Danielle Chen: Let’s go into the seq bucket thing. Because our problem is long context. How do you bucket?

[04:07] Yuki Sato: We extract prompt length (prefill tokens) and also we estimate expected decode length using either the max_tokens setting or observed from recent traffic. Then we classify into regimes.

[04:19] Yuki Sato: Simplifying a bit: short, medium, long context for prefill; and small vs large decode. For prefill, long context triggers kernels optimized for memory bandwidth and larger tile sizes. The key bug we saw in early testing was misclassifying “very long prompt, small decode” as “mixed,” which picked a kernel optimized for decode throughput but had worse prefill tail.

[04:42] Omar El-Sayed: And that’s exactly the p99 symptom: average ok, but at the long tail you get a 1.5x or 2x spike when you hit 20k+ tokens.

[04:52] Priya Nair: Are you actually measuring prefill vs decode times separately?

[04:56] Omar El-Sayed: Yes, internally we expose “prefill_ms” and “decode_ms” along with chosen kernel id. For canary we look at p95/p99 for each phase. Sometimes total looks fine but prefill is regressing and decode improves, which is not what you want for summarization.

[05:14] Alex Romero: In vLLM we’ve had issues where on L40S certain fused attention kernels are unstable. Do you have that kind of SKU weirdness?

[05:23] Yuki Sato: Yes, and that’s why GPU SKU is a first-class dimension. Some kernels are simply not available on certain CUDA/driver combos or have correctness issues under specific SM versions. So the selector has an explicit fallback hierarchy and a denylist.

[05:38] Danielle Chen: How do you normalize GPU SKU? Because in AWS it’s “p4d” or “p5”, and on our on-prem it’s like “A100-PCIe-80GB”. And then MIG.

[05:49] Ethan Park: Yeah, that comes up constantly. We have a normalization layer that maps cloud instance metadata and device properties into a canonical SKU string. For example, “A100-80GB-SXM4” vs “A100-80GB-PCIe”. We also tag MIG mode.

[06:05] Ethan Park: MIG is important because some kernels assume full GPU resources. So MIG gets treated as a separate SKU class for selection and for allow/deny.

[06:15] Priya Nair: We do use MIG sometimes for batch embeddings. Probably not for summarization, but we might. If MIG is on, do you just force a safe kernel?

[06:23] Yuki Sato: Typically yes. We’ll pick from a smaller candidate set that we’ve validated. And if you pin kernels for a pool, that overrides selection.

[06:32] Tom Bowers: Wait, you keep saying “pin.” Is that like a config knob or do we need support to do it?

[06:37] Ethan Park: It’s a config knob. For Hosted you’d do it via policy rules only in limited cases, but for Dedicated you can set an override: per model id, per GPU class, per region. And it’s hot reload, so you don’t need to restart the runtime.

[06:54] Omar El-Sayed: And there’s also a runtime CLI flag for debugging in non-prod, like “force_kernel=X” and “dump_selection_trace”. You wouldn’t use that in normal ops, but it helps reproduce.

[07:07] Danielle Chen: Ok. What do you log? Because from a security angle, we don’t want prompts in logs.

[07:13] Omar El-Sayed: We do not log prompt content. Telemetry includes model id, normalized sku, seq bucket (like “prefill_long”), selected kernel id, candidate set, and reason codes. No raw tokens.

[07:29] Tom Bowers: Candidate set sounds like it could be high cardinality.

[07:33] Omar El-Sayed: Yes, good call. We sample it. By default, detailed selection events are sampled at a low rate, and aggregated metrics are always on. Also we cap the number of candidates we emit.

[07:45] Priya Nair: So if we’re debugging a p99 spike, can we turn up sampling temporarily?

[07:50] Omar El-Sayed: Yes, with guardrails. You can increase sampling for a specific model or pool, time-bounded.

[08:00] Markus Klein: Just to keep us moving, maybe we switch to the long-context specifics. Danielle, can you share your exact concerns?

[08:08] Danielle Chen: Sure. We’ve seen in our own testing that kernels that are great at decode can be horrible at prefill once you cross like 16k. Our customers will notice if summarization goes from 4s to 8s for a subset. So we want confidence that your selector won’t “flip” at the wrong time.

[08:27] Yuki Sato: Yep. Our approach is: first, conservative thresholds for entering long-context regime. Second, explicit “long-context guardrail” where if prompt_len exceeds a hard cutoff we only consider kernels validated for long prefill. Third, fallback to a known-safe kernel if we detect instability.

[08:46] Alex Romero: Detect instability meaning errors? Or perf instability?

[08:50] Yuki Sato: Both. Errors like illegal memory access, but also perf anomalies like sudden latency increase beyond a threshold. The latter is more delicate because you don’t want flapping. So we mostly rely on rollout monitoring and allow/deny controls rather than automatic flapping.

[09:09] Omar El-Sayed: In practice, we’ll canary v2 for a small percentage and look at deltas in p95/p99 for prefill and total. If we see a spike, we disable v2 for that model+sku combination. That’s the “denylist” path.

[09:24] Priya Nair: How fast can you disable? Like minutes?

[09:27] Ethan Park: Minutes. The policy engine updates propagate typically under 2 minutes to all nodes in a region for Dedicated. Hosted is similar but depends on the layer you’re applying at.

[09:38] Tom Bowers: Who has authority? Us or Redwood?

[09:41] Ethan Park: For Dedicated, you do, via your admin role. Redwood can assist, but you can push the change.

[09:50] Markus Klein: Also for the POC we can set it so your team has that switch and we have a runbook.

[09:56] Danielle Chen: Great. Let’s talk GPU fleets. We currently have A100 80GB on-prem. In cloud we might use L40S for cost. We may evaluate H100 later. Does your selector handle all of those?

[10:10] Yuki Sato: Yes. A100, H100, L40S are in our validated set. L40S has some special cases; we’ve seen certain driver versions where a kernel is fine on one point release and not on another, so we have guardrails that disable v2 on known-bad driver/CUDA combos.

[10:29] Alex Romero: That’s interesting. We had that with TensorRT also. How do you know the driver version?

[10:34] Yuki Sato: We read it from the runtime environment, normalize it, and we match it against a small list. If it’s in the “known unstable” set, we either pick a safe kernel or disable v2 selection entirely.

[10:48] Priya Nair: Is that list public?

[10:50] Markus Klein: We can share what applies to your SKU. It changes, so we typically include it in release notes and a known-issues page.

[10:58] Tom Bowers: From compliance, we need to document any behavior that changes automatically. That’s why I ask.

[11:04] Ethan Park: The guardrail behavior is deterministic and versioned with runtime. It’s not like a remote kill switch that changes without you knowing. Policy changes are auditable.

[11:16] Danielle Chen: Good. Now, about benchmarking. What do you need from us? We can’t give you real prompts.

[11:22] Omar El-Sayed: You don’t need to. What we need is distributions: approximate input token histogram, output token histogram, concurrency levels, and any constraints like “must fit in 80GB.” If you can share a sanitized trace that includes just lengths, that’s perfect.

[11:41] Omar El-Sayed: For the benchmark matrix we want: model family you’ll use, like Llama 70B or 13B, seq buckets that match your workload (12k/16k/24k/32k), and GPUs: A100 and L40S at least. Then we run v1 vs v2 and compare p95/p99.

[11:59] Alex Romero: Are you using continuous batching? Because that changes the picture.

[12:03] Omar El-Sayed: Yes, continuous batching is on. And we also can pass scheduler hints into the selector about observed workload mix. But for the first run we can keep it simple and disable hints so we isolate kernel selection.

[12:18] Priya Nair: Wait, scheduler hints? Like it tells selector “this pool is mostly long context”?

[12:23] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly. It’s basically a rolling window of observed prompt lengths and decode lengths. The selector can choose a kernel that is more stable for that mix.

[12:35] Danielle Chen: But does that make it non-deterministic over time?

[12:39] Yuki Sato: The selection is deterministic given the hint input, but the hint input changes with traffic. So if you want strict replayability, you can either log the hint state or disable hint-based selection. For enterprise we often recommend disabling hints initially.

[12:57] Tom Bowers: For us, simpler is better.

[13:00] Markus Klein: Yeah, we can start with hints off, v2 gated, and then if we want to squeeze perf, we can add hints.

[13:08] Alex Romero: Can you talk about overhead? Like, does evaluating selector add latency? We’re very sensitive.

[13:14] Yuki Sato: It’s tiny. The selector is on the order of microseconds. The bigger risk is telemetry overhead if you emit too much. That’s why we sample. We also cache decisions per (model, sku, seq bucket) so repeated requests don’t even re-evaluate the full rule path.

[13:32] Omar El-Sayed: We have microbench data showing selector+telemetry stays under a small fraction of a millisecond at default sampling.

[13:42] Danielle Chen: Ok. Let’s talk failover. If the selected kernel is wrong, do you auto fallback mid-request?

[13:49] Yuki Sato: Not mid-request, no. That would be complex and potentially non-deterministic. The fallback hierarchy is applied at selection time. If a kernel fails at runtime (like an error), we fail the request and the system can retry with a safe kernel depending on policy. But we try to avoid that by denylists.

[14:09] Priya Nair: So if we see errors, we disable v2 quickly.

[14:12] Ethan Park: Exactly. And the rollback path is: disable v2 for model X on sku Y in region Z, or globally. That reverts to v1 mapping.

[14:25] Tom Bowers: And audit log shows who changed it.

[14:27] Ethan Park: Yep.

[14:30] Markus Klein: Maybe it’s helpful if we describe what “v2 rollout” looks like in Dedicated. Ethan?

[14:36] Ethan Park: Sure. You’d have a feature gate, off by default. Then you can enable for a single model version, in one region, for a small percentage of traffic. You can also do allowlist/denylist. If metrics regress beyond your thresholds, you flip it off. Changes are quick and reversible.

[14:56] Danielle Chen: When you say percentage, how do you route? Sticky per request? per pod?

[15:01] Ethan Park: Typically per pod or per shard of the pool, so it’s stable. We avoid per-request randomization for determinism and to reduce noise.

[15:12] Alex Romero: Great. Now, we also care about cost. L40S is cheaper. But long context on L40S might be slower. Does v2 help there?

[15:20] Omar El-Sayed: It can. L40S tends to have different sweet spots. With v2, we pick kernels tuned for that SKU which can reduce variance. It won’t magically beat H100, but it reduces p99 spikes and makes throughput more predictable.

[15:36] Priya Nair: How do you measure “predictable”?

[15:39] Omar El-Sayed: Standard deviation of per-request latency, plus p95/p99 gap. We also look at queueing time under load. Mis-selection can cause queueing cascades.

[15:52] Danielle Chen: That’s the big one. Cascades.

[15:55] Omar El-Sayed: Yep.

[15:58] (crosstalk)

[16:00] Markus Klein: Sorry, go ahead Danielle.

[16:02] Danielle Chen: No, just +1. We’ve seen that in Triton too, where one slow request blocks the batch.

[16:07] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly. So for your summarization workload, we’ll focus on the long-context prefill regime.

[16:15] Alex Romero: What models do you assume we’ll use? We’re currently evaluating Llama 3-ish 70B, and also a smaller 8B for some tasks.

[16:24] Markus Klein: Redwood supports those families. Yuki, anything on model-family tagging?

[16:30] Yuki Sato: Yeah. We tag by architecture based on model metadata/config. Sometimes people fine-tune and rename and the tag is missing. In v2 we have a classifier that inspects config fields to determine family. If it can’t, we fall back to a conservative default kernel set.

[16:50] Priya Nair: So “unknown model family” doesn’t break.

[16:53] Yuki Sato: Correct. You just get safe behavior.

[16:57] Tom Bowers: Safe means slower?

[16:59] Yuki Sato: Potentially slightly slower, yes, but stable.

[17:05] Danielle Chen: That’s fine for first launch.

[17:08] Markus Klein: Cool. Tom, anything else on security while we’re here?

[17:12] Tom Bowers: Just data retention and logging. You said no prompts in telemetry. For Dedicated, can logs stay in our account?

[17:19] Ethan Park: Yes. Dedicated can forward logs/metrics to your sink. We can also provide audit logs and integrate with your KMS in some setups. For this benchmark we’ll keep it minimal.

[17:32] Tom Bowers: Ok.

[17:34] Priya Nair: Back to the benchmark: what does “success” look like? Like, what deltas would you expect?

[17:40] Omar El-Sayed: It depends, but we generally aim for: no correctness regressions, and improved p95/p99 or at least reduced variance. For long-context, even a 10-15% improvement in p99 prefill is meaningful. Sometimes v2 is neutral but more stable across SKUs.

[17:58] Danielle Chen: Neutral average but improved tail is still a win.

[18:02] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly.

[18:05] Alex Romero: Do you have any customer story on long context?

[18:09] Markus Klein: We can share anonymized examples. But for now, the best is we run your workload distribution.

[18:17] Priya Nair: Agreed.

[18:20] Yuki Sato: Also, we’ll include a stress scenario: mixed workloads, where some requests are short and some are long. That’s where misclassification and batching interactions show up.

[18:34] Danielle Chen: Yep, because we’re not purely summarization. There’s chat-like stuff too.

[18:39] Omar El-Sayed: Great. We’ll include mixed.

[18:42] Markus Klein: Let’s do a quick “GPU inventory” check. Priya, you said A100 80s on-prem. In cloud, L40S maybe. Any H100?

[18:52] Priya Nair: Not today. H100 maybe next quarter. Also we have some A100 40GB, but we avoid them for long context.

[18:59] Yuki Sato: A100 40 vs 80 matters, yes. We treat that as separate SKU class.

[19:05] Alex Romero: And do you support splitting KV cache across GPUs? Not sure if relevant.

[19:10] Omar El-Sayed: We do tensor/pipeline parallel depending on model and pool config, but for kernel selection discussion we’re mostly within a GPU’s kernels. Multi-GPU changes throughput but kernels are still SKU-specific.

[19:25] Danielle Chen: Ok.

[19:27] Priya Nair: One more question: in vLLM, we sometimes had “it depends on batch size” for which kernel is best. Are you factoring batch size?

[19:35] Yuki Sato: Indirectly. We use sequence regime and, optionally, scheduler-provided batching hints. We don’t take “batch size” as a primary feature because it varies too quickly and makes selection unstable. But we choose kernels that are robust across a range of batch sizes for that regime.

[19:56] Omar El-Sayed: And if you have a dedicated pool that runs mostly one workload, the scheduler hints can help lock in the stable choice.

[20:07] Tom Bowers: That hint thing again. I’ll want it off in our first tests.

[20:11] Markus Klein: Understood.

[20:13] Alex Romero: Are you using Triton under the hood?

[20:16] Omar El-Sayed: No, we have our own serving runtime. Some kernels are built with CUDA and use Triton-language in places, but it’s not Triton Inference Server as the orchestration layer.

[20:28] Alex Romero: Got it.

[20:30] Danielle Chen: How do we debug if we see an anomaly? Like p99 spike at 24k.

[20:36] Omar El-Sayed: You’d look at dashboards: selection distribution by seq bucket, per-kernel latency histograms, and compare v1 vs v2. If v2 is picking “Kernel A” for long prefill and it correlates with spikes, we can denylist Kernel A for that SKU or adjust threshold. In emergencies you just disable v2.

[20:57] Ethan Park: And you can pin “safe kernel” for that model and pool.

[21:01] Priya Nair: Is there a notion of “known safe kernel” per family?

[21:05] Yuki Sato: Yes. There’s always a baseline kernel that we trust broadly. It may not be the fastest, but it’s stable.

[21:14] Danielle Chen: That’s basically what we want: a stable baseline and then an opt-in faster path.

[21:20] Markus Klein: Perfect. That aligns with how we ship v2.

[21:24] (brief silence)

[21:26] Markus Klein: Let me check time. We have about 35 minutes left. Anything else on the selection logic you want to poke at?

[21:33] Alex Romero: Yeah, how big is the candidate set? Like, do you have 2 kernels or 20?

[21:39] Yuki Sato: Depends on model family. Typically single-digit candidates, maybe 3-6 for attention. Then there’s additional kernels for other ops, but selection focus is attention path. We don’t want an explosion.

[21:56] Alex Romero: And you said you emit “reason codes.” What are those?

[22:01] Yuki Sato: Things like “gpu_sku_match,” “seq_bucket_long_prefill,” “kernel_denied_by_driver_guardrail,” “model_family_unknown_fallback.” It helps explain why you landed on a choice.

[22:16] Priya Nair: Nice.

[22:18] Tom Bowers: From an audit perspective, that’s also helpful. If we ever have to justify “why did we change behavior.”

[22:24] Ethan Park: Exactly.

[22:26] Danielle Chen: Ok, can we talk about how you’ll run the benchmark? Are we doing it ourselves or Redwood runs it?

[22:33] Markus Klein: Either. For quickest, we can run it in a Redwood Dedicated test pool and share results. If you need to run in your environment, we can provide the harness.

[22:46] Priya Nair: We probably want both. Because we need to trust it translates to our on-prem.

[22:52] Omar El-Sayed: For on-prem translation, the two biggest variables are GPU SKU and driver version. If those match, results correlate well. If they don’t, we’ll note differences.

[23:05] Danielle Chen: On-prem driver is usually behind, honestly.

[23:08] Yuki Sato: Then we should pay extra attention to the driver guardrails. If you’re on a known-problem version, we might recommend a safe kernel or staying on v1 until updated.

[23:22] Alex Romero: That’s fair.

[23:24] Markus Klein: Another question I’ve heard: “does v2 change outputs?” It shouldn’t. But maybe Omar can say something.

[23:31] Omar El-Sayed: Outputs should be identical. Kernels implement the same math within expected FP tolerances. We have correctness tests. If you enable deterministic modes, we keep nondeterminism minimized. But I’ll be candid: some kernels have different numerical behavior at the very low bits, which should not affect generation in practice. We gate anything that shows meaningful divergence.

[23:55] Priya Nair: We do have eval harness. We can check.

[23:58] Omar El-Sayed: Great. We can align on what evals matter.

[24:02] Danielle Chen: Ok. How do we coordinate? Should we send you distributions today?

[24:07] Markus Klein: Yeah, if you can send token length histograms and concurrency targets, we can prep the matrix.

[24:14] Ethan Park: Also confirm whether you need VPC peering for the Dedicated pool. It changes provisioning time.

[24:21] Priya Nair: For the benchmark, we can probably do it without VPC if we’re not sending data. But for later production, yes.

[24:29] Markus Klein: Great.

[24:31] Tom Bowers: One more: data residency. For now, US is fine.

[24:35] Markus Klein: Cool.

[24:38] Alex Romero: Since we mentioned competitors—Together, SageMaker endpoints—one thing they struggle with is “explain why performance changed.” Your telemetry seems to help.

[24:48] Omar El-Sayed: That’s the goal. The “selection trace” is basically “why.”

[24:53] Danielle Chen: Are dashboards included or extra?

[24:57] Markus Klein: In Dedicated, you get baseline dashboards. For deeper retention it can be an add-on, but for POC we’ll make sure you have what you need.

[25:06] Priya Nair: Ok.

[25:08] (crosstalk)

[25:09] Danielle Chen: Sorry, one more technical: does selection happen before compilation or after? Like, do you compile per kernel?

[25:17] Yuki Sato: Selection happens at runtime before execution, but after we know the model config. Some kernels have compiled variants. We keep a compilation cache keyed on model+kernel+sku and reuse.

[25:32] Alex Romero: So if kernel changes, you might hit compile overhead?

[25:36] Yuki Sato: Potentially on first use, yes. That’s another reason we avoid flapping and we cache decisions.

[25:44] Omar El-Sayed: And in canary we warm it up before measuring.

[25:49] Danielle Chen: Great.

[25:52] Priya Nair: I think we’ve got what we need. Can we recap deliverables?

[25:57] Markus Klein: Sure, let’s do a recap now and then we can use remaining time for any last Qs.

title: p99 latency regression on long-context requests after Runtime 1.21 canary (Kernel auto-selection v2) on L40S
text:
description:
Issue summary
- Customer reports p99 latency regression for long-context summarization workloads immediately after we enabled Runtime 1.21 canary on their Dedicated pool. Regression appears only for long-context requests (>= ~16k prompt tokens) and only on NVIDIA L40S.

Impact
- Customer-visible tail latency increase on long-context routes.
- Reported baseline (Runtime 1.20 / selector v1): p99 ~4.8–5.4s @ ~20k prompt tokens, 256–512 decode tokens.
- After canary (Runtime 1.21 / selector v2 enabled): p99 ~8.9–10.6s for same workload; p50/p90 mostly unchanged.
- No correctness issues reported. Error rate stable.

Customer context
- Northwind Analytics uses Redwood Dedicated for long-context summarization (document ingestion + map-reduce style prompts). Workload is bursty but within reserved throughput.

Environment
- Dedicated pool: nw-analytics-ded-01
- Region: us-east
- GPU SKU: NVIDIA L40S (SM89)
- Driver/CUDA: 550.54.14 / CUDA 12.4
- Runtime: 1.21.0-canary.3
- Feature: Kernel auto-selection v2 enabled via canary gate for Llama family

Steps to reproduce (as reported)
1) Send chat.completions with large prompts (~16k–32k tokens) and max_output_tokens 256–512.
2) Observe p99 latency increase vs previous runtime.
3) Short prompts (<4k) appear unaffected.

Observed signals
- Regressions correlate with selector choosing a different prefill kernel under v2 for the LONG seq bucket on L40S.
- Telemetry shows increased time in prefill stage; decode stage stable.

Example request IDs (customer-provided)
- req_7f2d5c8f2d8a4e1e (2026-02-20 18:12:44Z)
- req_3c19a0d91fb44b26 (2026-02-20 18:17:09Z)

Initial hypothesis
- Mis-selection in v2 for long-context prefill on L40S (SKU mapping + seq-bucket thresholds) causing fallback to a kernel variant with worse long-context characteristics on SM89.

Logs/snippets (redacted)
- Selection trace (sampled):
  - model_family=llama
  - seq_bucket=LONG
  - gpu_sku=l40s_sm89
  - chosen_prefill_kernel=fa3_fused_prefill_sm89 (candidate_score=0.71)
  - fallback_prefill_kernel=fa2_triton_prefill_sm89
  - chosen_decode_kernel=fa2_decode_sm89
- Perf counters summary (internal): prefill_ms +62% at 20k prompt; decode_ms within +/-3%.

Requested outcome
- Immediate mitigation (restore previous tail latency) and a safe path to re-enable v2 once fixed/guarded.

Root cause likely threshold bug in LONG bucket classification for mixed workloads + overly aggressive scoring weight for fa3 on SM89. We saw similar anomaly in earlier thread.

- Target PR: pr-28522-fix-regression-in-long-context-prefill-kernel-choice

Also recommend keeping deny in place for driver 550.54.14 until we complete validation (possible interaction with CUDA 12.4).
2026-02-22 16:30Z — Omar El-Sayed
Posted interim RCA summary to customer (via Markus):
- Regression introduced by selector v2 prefill kernel choice on L40S for long prompts
- Decode unaffected; no correctness impact
- Mitigation applied (v2 disabled + kernel deny)

Asked customer if they can provide a sanitized prompt-length histogram; will help confirm seq-bucket boundaries.
2026-02-24 11:12Z — Omar El-Sayed
Validated fix behavior in internal perf suite for L40S long-context scenarios. Plan:
- Keep customer-specific deny in place through 1.21 GA.
- Re-enable v2 only after patch release (1.21.1) and a canary on their pool with explicit rollback window.

Customer agreed to schedule test next week.

resolution:
Mitigated by disabling Kernel auto-selection v2 for affected Llama models on the customer’s Dedicated L40S pool (nw-analytics-ded-01, us-east) and adding a temporary kernel deny rule preventing selection of fa3_fused_prefill_sm89 for LONG seq bucket on L40S. Customer confirmed p99 latency returned to pre-canary baseline. No errors/correctness regressions observed.

next_steps:
Ship/land pr-28522 and include in Runtime 1.21.1 patch notes; ensure L40S long-context benchmarks are green before recommending re-enable.
Coordinate a controlled re-enable canary for Northwind (30–60 min window) with dashboards + explicit rollback trigger (p99 regression >10% for LONG bucket).
Audit selector v2 scoring defaults for SM89 and update known-issues list to call out L40S long-context prefill kernel sensitivity until validated.

title: Kernel Auto-Selection v2 — Override and Rollback Runbook
text:
## Purpose
This runbook describes how oncall can safely override or roll back **Kernel Auto-Selection v2** ("selector v2") when it causes tail-latency regressions, stability issues, or correctness risks. It covers:
- Disabling v2 by **model**, **GPU SKU**, and/or **region** (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)
- Pinning a specific kernel (temporary mitigation)
- Safe rollback procedure (fast + staged)
- Validation steps using dashboards and logs

**Primary goals:** restore p95/p99 latency and error rates to baseline while preserving correctness and preventing fleet-wide disruption.

---

## Scope / when to use
Use this runbook when any of the following are true during canary or production:
- p99 latency regression attributed to kernel selection (common: long-context prefill misclassification)
- Elevated runtime errors (CUDA illegal memory access, miscompiled kernel, launch failures) correlated with a chosen kernel/SKU
- Throughput instability or jitter that correlates with selection distribution changes
- Customer escalation requiring immediate mitigation (Dedicated/Private pools with constrained SKUs)

**Do not use** this runbook for general GPU/node instability, scheduler overload, or non-kernel runtime crashes unless kernel selection has been implicated.

---

## Ownership / escalation
**Oncall owns mitigation**, Runtime Kernels owns root cause.

- Runtime Oncall: #eng-oncall (primary)
- Runtime Kernels: #eng-runtime (paging if rollback required)
- SRE: #eng-sre (paging if SLO breach / incident)
- Releases: #eng-releases (if changes impact runtime 1.21 rollout windows)

Escalate immediately if:
- Any correctness regression suspected (bad outputs, determinism broken)
- Crash-looping exceeds 2% of pods in a region/pool
- You need to disable v2 globally in Hosted prod

---

## Preconditions / access
You need:
- Access to **Control Plane feature gates** and runtime config (prod breakglass if applicable)
- Dashboard access (Kernel Selection v2 Rollout dashboards)
- Log access for serving runtime pods

Tools referenced:
- `rwctl` (Redwood internal CLI)
- Runtime admin endpoint (read-only + safe config reload)

If `rwctl` is unavailable, use the Control Plane Console: **Console → Runtime → Feature Gates**.

---

## Definitions
- **v1**: existing kernel selection behavior (baseline)
- **v2**: kernel selection logic keyed on model family + sequence regime + GPU SKU
- **Gate**: enable/disable selector v2
- **Allowlist / denylist**: model- or SKU-scoped enablement rules
- **Pin**: force a specific kernel choice (override), bypassing selector ranking

### Canonical identifiers
Use canonical forms to avoid mismatches:
- **Region:** `us-east-1`, `us-west-2`, `eu-central-1`
- **GPU SKU:** normalized string e.g. `nvidia-a100-80gb`, `nvidia-h100-sxm`, `nvidia-l40s`
- **Model ID:** `llama-3-70b-instruct`, `mistral-large-2407`, `qwen2-72b-instruct`, `gemma-2-27b-it`

If SKU naming is ambiguous (MIG / cloud instance mapping), see: "GPU SKU normalization" in the debugging playbook.

---

## Quick decision tree (2 minutes)
1) **Is this isolated to one model OR one SKU OR one region?**
   - Yes → Disable v2 narrowly (model/SKU/region) OR pin kernel
   - No → Disable v2 at environment scope (Hosted prod or pool-wide) and page Runtime Kernels

2) **Are there runtime errors (not just latency)?**
   - Yes → Prefer **denylisting** the kernel/SKU combination (or disabling v2 for that SKU) rather than pinning.

3) **Is there a customer impact in Dedicated/Private?**
   - Yes → Prefer **pool-specific** disable or pin; avoid global Hosted changes unless needed.

---

## Primary levers
You have four safe mitigation levers (in preferred order):
1) **Disable v2 for a model in a region** (least blast radius)
2) **Disable v2 for a GPU SKU in a region/pool**
3) **Pin a kernel for a model+SKU+seq bucket** (fast workaround, higher risk)
4) **Disable v2 globally** (largest blast radius; requires notification)

---

## Step 0 — Confirm it is selector v2
Before changing gates, confirm correlation:

### A) Check selection distribution shift
Dashboard panel: **Selection distribution by kernel (model/SKU/seq bucket)**
- Look for a sudden rise in a kernel correlated with a latency spike.

### B) Confirm the request regime
Common signatures:
- Long-context prefill (e.g., prefill tokens > 8k) getting a kernel optimized for short prompts
- Mixed workloads: frequent switching between prefill/decode-heavy traffic

### C) Validate with logs (sample)
Search runtime logs for selection event:
- `kernel_selection_v2 decision` OR `selector_v2 chosen_kernel=`

If telemetry sampling is low, temporarily increase sampling for a narrow scope (model+region) only (see "Optional: increase telemetry sampling").

---

## Step 1 — Disable v2 (narrow scope)
Disabling v2 means: selector falls back to v1 behavior.

### 1A) Disable v2 for a specific model in a region (Hosted)
Use when a single model regresses.

Command:
- `rwctl runtime gates set kernel_autoselect_v2 --env hosted-prod --region us-east-1 --model llama-3-70b-instruct --value off`

Verify:
- `rwctl runtime gates get kernel_autoselect_v2 --env hosted-prod --region us-east-1 --model llama-3-70b-instruct`

Notes:
- Changes should propagate within ~2–5 minutes.
- If propagation stalls, trigger safe config reload (Step 4).

### 1B) Disable v2 for a GPU SKU in a region (Hosted)
Use when regressions are tied to a hardware type.

Command:
- `rwctl runtime gates set kernel_autoselect_v2 --env hosted-prod --region us-east-1 --gpu-sku nvidia-l40s --value off`

### 1C) Disable v2 for a Dedicated pool
Use when a Dedicated pool has a constrained GPU type or a customer escalation.

Command:
- `rwctl runtime gates set kernel_autoselect_v2 --env dedicated --pool ded-pool-northstar-a100 --value off`

If you need to scope it further:
- `rwctl runtime gates set kernel_autoselect_v2 --env dedicated --pool ded-pool-northstar-a100 --model qwen2-72b-instruct --value off`

### 1D) Disable v2 for Private deployments
Private customers may have pinned driver/CUDA versions; treat this as customer-impacting.

Command (if customer uses managed control plane):
- `rwctl runtime gates set kernel_autoselect_v2 --env private --tenant northwind-analytics --value off`

If the customer is air-gapped/on-prem, coordinate with Support/CS and provide them the config snippet (see "Private/on-prem config snippet").

---

## Step 2 — Denylist known-bad combinations (preferred for error spikes)
Use denylisting when the issue is tied to a **kernel+SKU** combination causing errors.

Example:
- Denylist `flash-attn-v3` on `nvidia-l40s` for all models in `us-east-1`.

Command:
- `rwctl runtime kernel-registry deny --env hosted-prod --region us-east-1 --gpu-sku nvidia-l40s --kernel flash-attn-v3 --reason "launch failures after 1.21 canary" --ttl 72h`

Notes:
- Prefer a TTL for emergency mitigation so it is automatically revisited.
- Denylisting should force selector v2 to choose the next safe fallback; if that is insufficient, disable v2 for that SKU.

---

## Step 3 — Pin a kernel (temporary mitigation)
Pinning is a faster workaround when v2 is enabled but picking the wrong kernel for a specific regime.

**Use pinning when:**
- Latency regression is due to mis-selection, not crashes
- You have a known-good kernel from prior benchmarks

**Avoid pinning when:**
- You see runtime errors / correctness concerns
- You are unsure which kernel is safe for that SKU

### 3A) Pin by model + SKU + sequence regime bucket
Common buckets:
- `prefill_short` (<= 2k prefill tokens)
- `prefill_medium` (2k–8k)
- `prefill_long` (> 8k)
- `decode_heavy` (high decode tokens)

Command:
- `rwctl runtime kernel-pin set --env hosted-prod --region us-east-1 --model llama-3-70b-instruct --gpu-sku nvidia-a100-80gb --seq-bucket prefill_long --kernel fused-prefill-v2 --ttl 24h --reason "p99 long-context regression; workaround"`

### 3B) Emergency runtime flag (last resort, debugging only)
If you need a one-off reproduction on a canary pod:
- Set the runtime flag via deployment override (do NOT do fleet-wide without Kernels approval):
  - `--force_kernel=fused-prefill-v2`
  - `--dump_kernel_selection=true`

This is for containment and debugging. Prefer config-based pins for production mitigation.

---

## Step 4 — Force config propagation / reload safely
Normally, changes propagate automatically. If dashboards do not reflect changes after ~5 minutes:

### 4A) Validate control plane state
- `rwctl runtime gates diff --env hosted-prod --region us-east-1 --model llama-3-70b-instruct`

### 4B) Trigger safe runtime config reload (no restart)
- `rwctl runtime config reload --env hosted-prod --region us-east-1 --service redwood-runtime`

### 4C) If pods are on stale config and reload fails
Use a **staged restart** (10% at a time). Coordinate with SRE if SLO is already violated.
- `rwctl kube rollout restart --cluster hosted-prod-us-east-1 --deploy redwood-runtime --max-unavailable 10%`

---

## Step 5 — Full rollback procedure (if needed)
A full rollback means: v2 is disabled broadly and selection behavior returns to v1.

### 5A) Rollback in Hosted (region-wide)
1. Announce in #eng-oncall and #eng-runtime: scope + reason.
2. Disable gate at region scope:
   - `rwctl runtime gates set kernel_autoselect_v2 --env hosted-prod --region us-east-1 --value off`
3. If impact spans multiple regions, roll back one region at a time unless error severity requires global.
4. Validate recovery (Step 6).

### 5B) Rollback in Dedicated pools
1. Disable for the affected pool:
   - `rwctl runtime gates set kernel_autoselect_v2 --env dedicated --pool <pool-name> --value off`
2. Notify Customer Success owner for the account if customer-facing.

### 5C) Rollback in Private
1. Disable for tenant (managed) or provide config snippet (on-prem).
2. Request customer to confirm their workload returns to baseline.

### 5D) Rollback authority / comms
- Oncall can roll back a region/pool when SLO impact is ongoing.
- If rolling back **all Hosted prod regions**, page Runtime Kernels lead (Hiro Tanaka) and SRE oncall.
- If rollback occurs during runtime release train activity, notify Release Engineering (Connor O'Brien).

---

## Step 6 — Validate recovery (must-do)
Validation should confirm both selection behavior and user-visible SLO improvement.

### 6A) Dashboards to check (minimum)
From **Kernel Selection v2 Rollout** dashboard:
- **p95/p99 latency** by model and region (compare to 1h baseline)
- **Error rate** (runtime errors, CUDA errors, request failures)
- **Selection distribution** (should reflect v1 or the new pinned kernel distribution)
- **Fallback rate** (spikes may indicate missing kernels; acceptable short-term but investigate)

From **Serving Runtime** dashboard:
- GPU utilization and queueing
- OOM / restart counts
- Throughput (tokens/sec) stability

### 6B) Log checks
- Confirm absence of repeated selection failures:
  - `selector_v2` errors should drop if v2 is disabled
- Confirm no elevated `CUDA error` or `illegal memory access` messages

### 6C) Canary comparison (if available)
If there is an active canary cohort:
- Compare v1 vs v2 cohorts for the same model/SKU/regime
- Ensure regression is resolved before re-enabling

### 6D) Success criteria (typical)
- p99 latency returns within **+3%** of pre-event baseline (or better)
- Error rate returns to baseline (no sustained elevated CUDA/runtime errors)
- Selection distribution matches intended override

---

## Optional — Increase selector telemetry sampling (narrowly)
If you cannot attribute the regression due to low sampling:

Command (model+region scoped):
- `rwctl runtime telemetry set kernel_selection --env hosted-prod --region us-east-1 --model llama-3-70b-instruct --sample-rate 0.05 --ttl 2h --reason "incident triage"`

Guardrails:
- Do not exceed 5% sampling without SRE approval (cardinality + ingestion cost).
- Ensure telemetry fields do not include user prompts (PII policy).

---

## Private/on-prem config snippet (customer-facing)
If a Private on-prem customer needs a manual config override, provide this snippet (do not paste internal-only fields):

Example (YAML):
- `kernel_auto_selection_v2: "off"`

If they need a narrower override:
- `kernel_auto_selection_v2_model_overrides: "llama-3-70b-instruct=off"`

If they need a temporary pin:
- `kernel_pin: "model=llama-3-70b-instruct,gpu=nvidia-a100-80gb,seq=prefill_long,kernel=fused-prefill-v2"`

Always include:
- Scope (which model/SKU/region)
- Expected effect
- TTL / when to remove

---

## Common failure modes and recommended actions
1) **Long-context p99 spikes** (prefill > 8k)
- Action: disable v2 for model in region OR pin known-good long-prefill kernel

2) **Errors on a single SKU** (e.g., L40S)
- Action: denylist the kernel on that SKU OR disable v2 for that SKU

3) **Selection nondeterminism suspicion** (inconsistent kernel chosen for same inputs)
- Action: disable v2 for affected scope; page Runtime Architecture (Noah Patel / Jordan Lee)

4) **Dashboard alert noise due to metric cardinality**
- Action: validate actual latency/error; coordinate with Observability (Allison Grant)

---

## Post-mitigation follow-ups (required)
Within 24 hours of any production override/rollback:
1. File or update a tracking issue in the v2 epic with:
   - Scope (model/SKU/region/pool)
   - Symptoms (latency/error metrics)
   - Mitigation taken (gate off / denylist / pin)
   - Validation results
2. Update **Known Issues & Workarounds** page if this is a repeatable condition.
3. If a pin/denylist was added with TTL, set a reminder to reassess before expiry.
4. If customer-facing (Dedicated/Private), summarize in the customer ticket and share the safe removal plan.

---

## Appendix A — Reference: typical kernel names
(Names may differ by build; use the registry list command to confirm availability.)

List kernels for a SKU:
- `rwctl runtime kernel-registry list --env hosted-prod --region us-east-1 --gpu-sku nvidia-a100-80gb`

Common kernels:
- `flash-attn-v3`
- `triton-sdp`
- `xformers-attn`
- `fused-prefill-v2`
- `paged-kv-decode-v1`

---

## Appendix B — Safe revert of a temporary override
If you applied a temporary pin or denylist:

Remove pin:
- `rwctl runtime kernel-pin clear --env hosted-prod --region us-east-1 --model llama-3-70b-instruct --gpu-sku nvidia-a100-80gb --seq-bucket prefill_long`

Remove denylist entry:
- `rwctl runtime kernel-registry deny clear --env hosted-prod --region us-east-1 --gpu-sku nvidia-l40s --kernel flash-attn-v3`

Re-enable v2 (only after perf is validated):
- `rwctl runtime gates set kernel_autoselect_v2 --env hosted-prod --region us-east-1 --model llama-3-70b-instruct --value on`

---

## Changelog
- 2026-02-21: Added Dedicated/Private examples, TTL guidance for denylist/pins, and staged restart guidance.
- 2026-02-04: Updated telemetry sampling guardrails and validation thresholds.
- 2026-01-18: Initial version for runtime 1.21 canary and staged rollout.

title: Northwind Analytics - technical deep dive: tail latency + KV cache behavior
text:
transcript:
MEETING HEADER (Fireflies)
Title: Northwind Analytics - technical deep dive: tail latency + KV cache behavior
Date: Jan 14, 2026
Time: 10:06 AM - 11:02 AM PT
Duration: 56 minutes
Participants:
- Nikhil Sharma (Redwood Inference)
- Omar El-Sayed (Redwood Inference)
- Mateo Alvarez (Redwood Inference)
- Sean Gallagher (Redwood Inference)
- Allison Grant (Redwood Inference)
- Priya Desai (Northwind Analytics)
- Evan Brooks (Northwind Analytics)
- Jing Wu (Northwind Analytics)
- Tomás Alvarez (Northwind Analytics)

AUTO-GENERATED SUMMARY
Northwind described burst-driven p99 latency spikes in chat-style workloads with mixed prompt lengths, plus occasional GPU OOM / request shedding on their current stack. Redwood walked through how KV cache allocation patterns and fragmentation can create tail latency under churn, especially when long-lived sessions coexist with short requests and cancellation/retry behavior. Redwood outlined planned runtime improvements: fragmentation measurement, budgeted compaction integrated with the scheduler, and tier-aware eviction (LRU-ish) with kill-switches and observability. Discussion covered what signals to capture (decode vs prefill timing, allocator arena health, bytes moved), and how to run a benchmark that reproduces Northwind’s traffic shape.

TOPICS
- What “tail latency” looks like in mixed-length decode workloads
- KV cache basics (pages/blocks), long-lived allocations, churn, cancellations
- Fragmentation: why it happens, what it costs, why it triggers at the wrong time
- Compaction: incremental vs background, budgets, scheduler integration
- Eviction policy: tier-aware + LRU, pinned sessions, prefix caching interactions
- Guardrails: backpressure, kill-switch, rollback criteria, metrics
- Benchmark ask + what Redwood needs from Northwind

QUESTIONS (captured)
- Can Redwood separate prefill latency from decode latency per request? (Yes, and we can share how we instrument it.)
- How does compaction avoid stalling decode? (Budgeted moves tied to scheduler boundaries; can pause under load.)
- Does eviction affect correctness or output stability? (No correctness change; could impact cache hit rates, which affects latency/cost.)
